---
title: "Plots with matplotlib and plotnine"
---

A basemap goes under your data: `m.add_to(ax)` in matplotlib,
`ggplot(df) + m` in plotnine. The plot gives what a basemap on its own needs
from you: the extent (the axes' limits), the CRS (the basemap is warped into
it, so it lines up with the data), the image size (the axes) and the dpi (on
screen 96 x the screen's pixel ratio, in `savefig(dpi=300)` 300, in PDF and
SVG 300). It renders when the figure is drawn, so panning, zooming and
saving draw it afresh, and it credits the provider in the corner.

```{python}
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message=".*centroid.*")

import basemapper as bm
import geodatasets
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

nc = gpd.read_file(geodatasets.get_path("geoda.sids"))
```

## matplotlib

`m.add_to(ax)` draws under what the axes already show, and returns the
basemap's artist. Plain axes carry no CRS, so give it the data's with
`crs=` (cartopy GeoAxes are read). `bm.add_basemap(ax, style, ...)` is the
same in one call: `bm.add_basemap(ax, "OpenFreeMap.Positron", crs=nc.crs)`
is `bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)`. Both take
the layer's own settings, `alpha` and `attribution`, so use whichever reads
better; this guide mostly uses `add_to()`.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "matplotlib choropleth of North Carolina's counties by sudden infant deaths per 1,000 births in 1979, in orange-red shades over the light grey OpenFreeMap Positron basemap, with a colour bar."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.assign(rate=nc.SID79 / nc.BIR79 * 1000).plot(
    ax=ax, column="rate", cmap="OrRd", alpha=0.8, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2,
    legend=True, legend_kwds={"label": "SIDS per 1,000 births, 1979", "shrink": 0.7},
)
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Projected data

The basemap is drawn in Web Mercator and warped into the axes' CRS, so it
lines up with data in any CRS. Here North Carolina's state plane
(EPSG:32119), with the counties' centroids sized by births:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "North Carolina in its state plane projection: county outlines and orange circles at the counties' centres sized by births in 1974, over Esri's World Topo Map, warped to the projection so roads and towns line up with the counties."
nc_sp = nc.to_crs(32119)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc_sp.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.15", linewidth=0.3)
nc_sp.centroid.plot(ax=ax, markersize=nc_sp.BIR74 / 300, color="#D96E34", alpha=0.7)
bm.add_basemap(ax, "Esri.WorldTopoMap", crs=nc_sp.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### A quieter basemap

For a data map, a basemap often reads better without its labels, faded, or
with only some of its features. Filters belong to the style (see [Stacking,
labels and features](04-layers.qmd)); `alpha` fades the layer:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "North Carolina's counties coloured by the share of births to non-white mothers in 1974, on a viridis scale, over a faded OpenFreeMap Liberty basemap without labels, roads or rail."
quiet = bm.style("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", features=["-labels", "-roads", "-rail"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.assign(share=nc.NWBIR74 / nc.BIR74).plot(
    ax=ax, column="share", cmap="viridis", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2, legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Share of births, non-white, 1974", "shrink": 0.7},
)
bm.basemap(quiet).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, alpha=0.6)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Sharpness and detail

Each has one place:

- **Sharpness** is the figure's dpi: `savefig(dpi=300)`, the figure's `dpi`
  on screen, or 300 dpi for PDF and SVG. It makes the map sharper and
  changes nothing else. A basemap's `dpi` is an error in a plot.
- **What the map shows** goes in `basemap()`: either `zoom` (the detail) or
  `symbol_scale` (the size of lines, labels and icons). Each sets the other,
  so give one. With neither, the symbol scale is 1.

[Sharpness, detail and size](06-sharpness.qmd) shows each of them side by
side, what changes with the axes size, and which to set for what you want.

```python
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", symbol_scale=0.8).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)  # smaller labels, more detail
fig.savefig("nc.png", dpi=300)       # sharpness only
bm.last_rendering().zoom             # the zoom it drew at
```

A `zoom` of your own gives a chosen detail:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Central North Carolina around Raleigh, Durham and Cary in OpenFreeMap Liberty at zoom 8: county outlines over highways, lakes and town names."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.2", linewidth=0.3)
ax.set_xlim(-80, -77.5)
ax.set_ylim(35, 36.5)
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", zoom=8).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

The basemap follows the axes, so setting their limits zooms it in, with
detail to match:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Satellite imagery of North Carolina's Outer Banks and Pamlico Sound, with yellow county outlines and white county names such as Dare, Hyde and Tyrrell."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.2))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="yellow", linewidth=1)
for _, row in nc.iterrows():
    p = row.geometry.representative_point()
    if -76.9 < p.x < -75.4 and 35.0 < p.y < 36.0:
        ax.annotate(row.NAME, (p.x, p.y), color="white", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-76.9, -75.4)
ax.set_ylim(35.0, 36.0)
bm.add_basemap(ax, "Esri.WorldImagery", crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Clipping

`clip` draws the basemap only inside a layer's polygons, or outside them
with `bm.outside()`. In a plot, the plot still gives the extent: the clip is
a mask. Here the state in colour over a faded copy:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Satellite imagery of North Carolina in full colour inside the state's counties and faded outside them, with thin white county outlines."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.2)
bm.basemap("Esri.WorldImagery").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, alpha=0.35, attribution=False)
bm.basemap("Esri.WorldImagery", clip=nc).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Credits

The credit line is on by default. `attribution=False` turns it off;
`get_attribution()` returns the text, for a caption:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "North Carolina's county outlines in blue over Esri's light grey canvas basemap, with the provider's credit as small text below the map instead of in its corner."
gray = bm.basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="steelblue", linewidth=0.4)
gray.add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, attribution=False)
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.text(0.98, 0.02, bm.get_attribution(gray), ha="right", fontsize=6, color="0.4")
```

## plotnine

Add a basemap to a plotnine plot with `+`, like a layer. Two ways put the
same layer in the plot:

| | Takes | Use it |
|---|---|---|
| `+ bm.basemap(...)` | what the map is: the style, `zoom` or `symbol_scale`, `clip`, `fetch` | usually |
| `+ bm.geom_basemap(...)` | all of that, plus the layer's own settings: `alpha`, `attribution` and `crs` | to fade the basemap, change its credit line, or give the CRS |

plotnine has no spatial coordinates: the basemap reads the CRS of a
GeoDataFrame's data, else takes `geom_basemap(crs=...)`, else longitude /
latitude. `geom_basemap()` also takes a basemap you already made:
`bm.geom_basemap(m, alpha=0.5)`.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "plotnine map of North Carolina's counties in shades of blue by births in 1979, with white borders, over the light grey OpenFreeMap Positron basemap, and a legend."
from plotnine import aes, geom_map, ggplot, scale_fill_distiller, theme, theme_void

(
    ggplot(nc)
    + bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron")
    + geom_map(aes(fill="BIR79"), alpha=0.75, color="white", size=0.2)
    + scale_fill_distiller(type="seq", palette="Blues", direction=1, name="Births, 1979")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

Raster and vector basemaps, stacks and filters work the same way; here
shaded relief under a vector basemap's labels:

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "plotnine map of North Carolina: Esri's shaded relief with OpenFreeMap Liberty's place labels on top, county outlines, and orange dots at the counties' centres sized by births in 1974, with a legend."
from plotnine import geom_point, scale_size_area

relief = ["Esri.WorldShadedRelief", bm.style("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", features="labels")]
centroids = nc.assign(x=nc.centroid.x, y=nc.centroid.y)

(
    ggplot(centroids)
    + bm.basemap(relief)
    + geom_map(fill=None, color="#333333", size=0.25)
    + geom_point(aes("x", "y", size="BIR74"), color="#D96E34", alpha=0.7)
    + scale_size_area(max_size=6, name="Births, 1974")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

## Saving

`savefig()` and plotnine's `save()` save the whole figure, and draw the
basemap again at the file's dpi: the same map, sharp at that resolution. A
PDF or SVG gets it at 300 dpi.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# matplotlib
fig.savefig("nc.png", dpi=300)
fig.savefig("nc.pdf")

# plotnine
p = ggplot(nc) + bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron") + geom_map(fill=None)
p.save("nc-plotnine.png", width=7, height=4, dpi=300)
p.save("nc-plotnine.pdf", width=7, height=4)
```

To save a basemap without a plot (PNG, SVG, GeoTIFF, JPEG or GeoPDF), see
[Saving a basemap on its own](01-get-started.qmd#saving-a-basemap-on-its-own).
